narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your undergraduate GPA, your first-year law school grades, and your third-year law school grades. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 3.10 it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic preparation for the exam. Your first-year performance in law school was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. Placing in the 5th decile is lower than the 6th-decile average among accepted students, indicating you were not in the top half of your class that year.

Your third-year grades worked in the opposite direction. Ranking in the 7th decile is stronger than the 5.8 average of accepted students, so this factor helped push the prediction back toward passing. However, it was not enough to overcome the earlier academic signals.

Your LSAT score of 37 was almost identical to the accepted average, your upper-middle family income is the most common bracket among accepted students, and your full-time status matches the overwhelming majority of successful applicants. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record or gaining targeted bar-exam support before reapplying. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a strong bar-prep program, or waiting until you have a clearer record of success in demanding academic settings.
